raw_text: {"schema_version":"chat_response_v1","response_type":"answer","answer_text":"No. Binding at an allosteric site does not necessarily inhibit an enzyme, because allosteric regulators can also be activators. [ev_001] [ev_002] An allosteric inhibitor binds to a location other than the active site and induces a conformational change that reduces the enzyme's affinity for its substrate. [ev_001] This change can reduce enzyme activity because the enzyme no longer effectively catalyzes the conversion of substrate to product. [ev_005] An allosteric activator binds to a location away from the active site and induces a conformational change that increases the affinity of the active site for its substrate. [ev_001] [ev_002] In terms of shape, an allosteric inhibition indirectly induces a conformational change to the active site so that the substrate no longer fits, whereas an allosteric activation modifies the shape of the active site to allow a better fit of the substrate. [ev_002] So the inhibitor lowers substrate binding and activity, while the activator raises substrate binding. [ev_001] [ev_002] [ev_005] Allosteric effectors may increase or decrease enzyme activity depending on the prevailing conditions, so the effect on activity is not fixed by the binding site alone.
